SPOUSAL / COMMUNITY LIABILITY FOR DEBTS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's default statutory rules for when a married person's community property, earnings, or separate property can be used to satisfy a debt that the other spouse incurred, before or during the marriage. These are the rules that apply automatically, under Family Code sections 910 through 916, in the absence of a premarital agreement, postnuptial agreement, or other written agreement that changes them. It concerns Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee.

This document is limited to the statutory default liability scheme as between a debtor spouse, the other spouse, and an outside creditor. It is not this project's Premarital Agreement document, which addresses how spouses may contractually reallocate responsibility for debts between themselves -- a valid agreement under the Uniform Premarital Agreement Act can change what this document describes. It is also not this project's Family Code section 2640/2641 reimbursement documents, which address tracing and reimbursing a spouse's separate-property contributions toward the acquisition of community assets at the time of division, a different question from whether an outside creditor can reach property to satisfy a debt in the first place. This document states what the statutes provide; it does not determine whether any particular debt, account, or item of property of Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Casey Lee is or is not reachable by a creditor, which depends on the specific facts and, where disputed, is decided by a court.

COMMUNITY ESTATE'S DEFAULT LIABILITY FOR EITHER SPOUSE'S DEBT
Under Family Code section 910, except as otherwise expressly provided by statute, the community estate is liable for a debt incurred by either spouse before or during the marriage. This liability applies regardless of which spouse has management and control of the property, and regardless of whether one or both spouses are parties to the debt or to a judgment on the debt. For this purpose, the statute defines "during marriage" to exclude the period after the date of separation and before a judgment of dissolution of marriage or legal separation. A separate section of the same statutory chapter, Family Code section 912, extends this same liability rule to quasi-community property, providing that quasi-community property is liable to the same extent, and treated the same in all other respects, as community property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) Except as otherwise expressly provided by statute, the community estate is liable for a debt incurred by either spouse before or during marriage, regardless of which spouse has the management and control of the property and regardless of whether one or both spouses are parties to the debt or to a judgment for the debt. (b) “During marriage” for purposes of this section does not include the period after the date of separation, as defined in Section 70, and before a judgment of dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 910(a)-(b), community estate's liability for a debt incurred by either spouse before or during marriage, and the definition of "during marriage" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=910.)
  "quasi-community property is liable to the same extent, and shall be treated the same in all other respects, as community property."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 912, quasi-community property is liable to the same extent, and treated the same in all other respects, as community property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=912.)
  Known gap: Family Code sections 910(a) and 910(b) are subdivisions of the same enacted section, and section 912 is a companion provision within the same statutory chapter (General Rules of Liability, sections 910-916); the citations below are not independent sources of one another. Section 910(a) begins "Except as otherwise expressly provided by statute" -- this document does not catalog every statutory exception to the general community-liability rule (for example, the earnings-protection and necessaries-of-life provisions addressed in this document's other clauses are themselves such exceptions), and a reader should not assume the general rule stated here applies without checking for an applicable exception.

DEFAULT RULE: SEPARATE PROPERTY LIABLE ONLY FOR ITS OWNER'S OWN DEBTS
Family Code section 913 states the default rule for a married person's own separate property: it is liable for a debt that person incurred before or during the marriage. Except as otherwise provided by statute, section 913 also states the converse default rule protecting the other spouse: a married person's separate property is not liable for a debt incurred by that person's spouse before or during the marriage. The statute further provides that a person's joinder in, or consent to, an encumbrance of community estate property to secure a debt the person's spouse incurred does not, by itself, subject that person's separate property to liability for the debt, unless the joining or consenting person also incurred the debt.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) The separate property of a married person is liable for a debt incurred by the person before or during marriage."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 913(a), a married person's own separate property is liable for a debt that person incurred before or during marriage (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=913.)
  "(b) Except as otherwise provided by statute: (1) The separate property of a married person is not liable for a debt incurred by the person’s spouse before or during marriage. (2) The joinder or consent of a married person to an encumbrance of community estate property to secure payment of a debt incurred by the person’s spouse does not subject the person’s separate property to liability for the debt unless the person also incurred the debt."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 913(b), a married person's separate property is not liable for the other spouse's debt, and joinder in an encumbrance alone does not create such liability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=913.)
  Known gap: Family Code section 913(a) and section 913(b) (including its two numbered clauses) are subdivisions of the same enacted section; the citations below are not independent sources of one another. Section 913(b) begins "Except as otherwise provided by statute" -- section 914, addressed in this document's companion clause on necessaries of life, is itself one such statutory exception to the protection described here, and this document does not catalog any other exception to section 913's default rules.

PROTECTION OF A SPOUSE'S EARNINGS FROM THE OTHER SPOUSE'S PREMARITAL DEBT
Family Code section 911 provides a specific protection for a married person's own earnings against a debt the person's spouse incurred before marriage. Under this section, the earnings of a married person during marriage are not liable for a debt incurred by the person's spouse before marriage. That protection continues after the earnings are paid to the person, for as long as the earnings are held in a deposit account over which the spouse has no right of withdrawal and are not commingled with other community estate property, other than an insignificant amount. The statute separately defines "earnings" as compensation for personal services performed, whether as an employee or otherwise, and defines "deposit account" by reference to the Commercial Code.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) The earnings of a married person during marriage are not liable for a debt incurred by the person’s spouse before marriage. After the earnings of the married person are paid, they remain not liable so long as they are held in a deposit account in which the person’s spouse has no right of withdrawal and are uncommingled with other property in the community estate, except property insignificant in amount."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 911(a), a married person's earnings during marriage are not liable for a debt the spouse incurred before marriage, subject to conditions on how the earnings are held (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=911.)
  Known gap: This clause draws only on Family Code section 911. It is included as a distinct exception to the general community-liability rule of section 910 (addressed in this document's companion clause), which would otherwise make the community estate -- including a spouse's earnings once they become community property -- liable for a premarital debt of either spouse. Section 911 protects only earnings meeting its own conditions (held in a segregated, no-withdrawal-right deposit account); it does not protect earnings once commingled beyond an insignificant amount, and it does not apply to a debt a spouse incurs during the marriage, which is governed by section 910's general rule instead.

EXCEPTION: PERSONAL LIABILITY FOR A SPOUSE'S DEBT FOR NECESSARIES OF LIFE
Family Code section 914 creates an exception to section 913's default protection of a nondebtor spouse's separate property. Notwithstanding section 913, a married person is personally liable for two categories of debt incurred by the person's spouse during the marriage: a debt incurred for necessaries of life of the spouse before the date of separation, and, except as provided in Family Code section 4302, a debt incurred for common necessaries of life of the spouse after the date of separation. Where a person's separate property is applied to satisfy a debt for which the person is personally liable under this section, the statute grants a right of reimbursement to the extent that nonexempt community estate property or the spouse's own separate property was available at the time but was not applied to the debt instead.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) Notwithstanding Section 913, a married person is personally liable for the following debts incurred by the person’s spouse during marriage: (1) A debt incurred for necessaries of life of the person’s spouse before the date of separation of the spouses. (2) Except as provided in Section 4302, a debt incurred for common necessaries of life of the person’s spouse after the date of separation of the spouses."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 914(a), personal liability for a spouse's debt for necessaries of life, before and after separation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=914.)
  "(b) The separate property of a married person may be applied to the satisfaction of a debt for which the person is personally liable pursuant to this section. If separate property is so applied at a time when nonexempt property in the community estate or separate property of the person’s spouse is available but is not applied to the satisfaction of the debt, the married person is entitled to reimbursement to the extent such property was available."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 914(b), the reimbursement right when separate property is applied to a necessaries debt while other available property was not (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=914.)
  Known gap: Family Code section 914(a) and section 914(b) are subdivisions of the same enacted section; the citations below are not independent sources of one another. Section 914 does not itself define "necessaries of life" or "common necessaries of life"; this document does not supply a definition of that statutory term, and whether a particular debt qualifies is a fact-specific determination the statute's text does not resolve. Section 914(a)(2) is itself made subject to a further statutory exception, Family Code section 4302, which this document does not separately address. Section 914(c)-(d) (not quoted here) set a special statute-of-limitations rule for this liability if the debtor spouse dies, which this document does not otherwise cover.

LIABILITY OF PROPERTY AFTER DIVISION OF THE COMMUNITY ESTATE
Family Code section 916 addresses what happens to this liability scheme once the community and quasi-community estate has been divided in a dissolution or legal separation proceeding. Notwithstanding any other provision of this statutory chapter, after that division: the separate property a married person owned at the time of division, and the property the person received in the division, remains liable for a debt that person incurred before or during the marriage, and the person remains personally liable for it, whether or not the debt was assigned for payment by the person's spouse in the division. Conversely, that same property is not liable for a debt incurred by the person's spouse before or during the marriage, and the person is not personally liable for it, unless the debt was assigned for payment by the person in the division -- though the statute notes this does not affect the liability of property for satisfying a lien already on it. Where a debt was assigned to the person in the division and the person's property is later applied to satisfy a money judgment on that debt, the statute gives the person a right of reimbursement from the spouse to whom the debt was assigned, with interest at the legal rate, plus reasonable attorney's fees incurred in enforcing that reimbursement right.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) Notwithstanding any other provision of this chapter, after division of community and quasi-community property pursuant to Division 7 (commencing with Section 2500): (1) The separate property owned by a married person at the time of the division and the property received by the person in the division is liable for a debt incurred by the person before or during marriage and the person is personally liable for the debt, whether or not the debt was assigned for payment by the person’s spouse in the division. (2) The separate property owned by a married person at the time of the division and the property received by the person in the division is not liable for a debt incurred by the person’s spouse before or during marriage, and the person is not personally liable for the debt, unless the debt was assigned for payment by the person in the division of the property. Nothing in this paragraph affects the liability of property for the satisfaction of a lien on the property."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 916(a), post-division liability of a person's separate property and awarded property for the person's own debts versus the spouse's debts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=916.)
  "(b) If property of a married person is applied to the satisfaction of a money judgment pursuant to subdivision (a) for a debt incurred by the person that is assigned for payment by the person’s spouse, the person has a right of reimbursement from the person’s spouse to the extent of the property applied, with interest at the legal rate, and may recover reasonable attorney’s fees incurred in enforcing the right of reimbursement."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 916(b), reimbursement right when a person's property satisfies a judgment on a debt assigned to the spouse in the division (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=916.)
  Known gap: Family Code section 916(a) (including its three numbered paragraphs) and section 916(b) are subdivisions of the same enacted section; the citations below are not independent sources of one another. Paragraph (a)(3)'s judgment-enforcement mechanics are paraphrased in this clause's body rather than reproduced as a separate quoted citation. This section applies only after an actual division of the community and quasi-community estate under Division 7 (commencing with Family Code section 2500); it does not describe the liability rules that apply before such a division, which are addressed in this document's other clauses.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT -- NOT A COURT FILING
I acknowledge that I have read and understand this information sheet describing California's default statutory rules on spousal and community liability for debts under Family Code sections 910 through 916, as it relates to Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee. This document is educational only. It does not itself determine whether any specific debt, account, or item of property is reachable by any creditor, and it is not filed with any court.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: _________________________

Signature of Morgan Casey Lee: _________________________
